
## broadcast Package Overview {.unnumbered}


### Description

broadcast: <br />
'Numpy'-Like Broadcasted Operations for Atomic and Recursive Arrays with Minimal Dependencies. <br /> <br />
Implements efficient broadcasted operations for atomic and recursive arrays.

Besides linking to 'Rcpp', 'broadcast' does not depend on, vendor, link to, include, or otherwise use any external libraries;
'broadcast' was essentially made from scratch and can be installed out-of-the-box.

The implementations available in 'broadcast' include, but are not limited to, the following:


<ol>
<li> Broadcasted element-wise operations on any 2 arrays;
they support a large set of relational-, arithmetic-, Boolean-, string- and bit-wise operations.

</li>
<li> A faster, more memory efficient, and broadcasted abind-like function, for binding arrays along an arbitrary dimension.

</li>
<li> Broadcasted ifelse- and apply-like functions.

</li>
<li> The <code>acast()</code> function, for casting/pivoting an array into a new dimension.

</li>
<li> Simple linear algebra functions for statistics.

</li></ol>

The functions in the 'broadcast' package strive to minimize computation time and memory usage (which is not just good for efficient computing, but also for the environment).<br /> <br />

### Functions

<b>Functions for broadcasted element-wise binary operations</b> <br />
'broadcast' provides a set of functions for broadcasted element-wise binary operations
with broadcasting. <br />
These functions use an API similar to the outer function. <br />
<br />
The following functions for binary operations are available:


<ul>
<li> [bc.b](bc.b.qmd): Boolean (i.e. logical) operations;

</li>
<li> [bc.i](bc.i.qmd): integer arithmetic and relational operations;

</li>
<li> [bc.d](bc.d.qmd): decimal arithmetic and relational operations;

</li>
<li> [bc.cplx](bc.cplx.qmd): complex arithmetic and (in)equality operations;

</li>
<li> [bc.str](bc.str.qmd): string (in)equality, concatenation, and distance operations;

</li>
<li> [bc.raw](bc.raw.qmd): byte- and relational operations for vectors/arrays of type <code>raw</code>;

</li>
<li> [bc.bit](bc.bit.qmd): BIT-WISE operations, supporting the <code>raw</code> and <code>integer</code> types;

</li>
<li> [bc.list](bc.list.qmd): apply any 'R' function to 2 recursive arrays with broadcasting. <br /> <br />

</li></ul>

<b><code>bind_array()</code></b> <br />
'broadcast' provides the [bind_array](bind_array.qmd) function,
to bind arrays along an arbitrary dimension,
with support for broadcasting. <br />
<br />
The API of <code>bind_array()</code> is inspired by the fantastic
<code>abind::abind()</code> function
by Tony Plare &amp; Richard Heiberger (2016). <br />
But <code>bind_array()</code> differs considerably from <code>abind::abind</code>
in the following ways:


<ul>
<li> <code>bind_array()</code> allows for broadcasting,
while <code>abind::abind</code> does not support broadcasting.

</li>
<li> <code>bind_array()</code> differs from <code>abind::abind</code>
in that it can handle recursive arrays properly <br />
(the <code>abind::abind</code> function would unlist everything to atomic arrays,
ruining the structure).

</li>
<li> <code>bind_array()</code> is generally faster than <code>abind::abind</code>,
as <code>bind_array()</code> relies heavily on 'C' and 'C++' code.

</li>
<li> unlike <code>abind::abind</code>,
<code>bind_array()</code> only binds (atomic/recursive) arrays and matrices. <br />
<code>bind_array()</code>does not attempt to convert things to arrays when they are not arrays,
but will give an error instead. <br />
This saves computation time and prevents unexpected results.

</li>
<li> <code>bind_array()</code> has more streamlined naming options,
compared to <code>abind::abind</code>. <br /> <br />

</li></ul>

<b><code>acast()</code></b> <br />
'broadcast' provides the [acast](acast.qmd) function,
for casting (i.e. pivoting) an array into a new dimension. <br />
Useful for, for example, computing <b>grouped</b> broadcasted operations. <br />
<br />

<b>General functions</b> <br />
'broadcast' also comes with 2 general broadcasted functions:


<ul>
<li> [bc_ifelse](bc_ifelse.qmd): Broadcasted version of ifelse.

</li>
<li> [bcapply](bcapply.qmd): Broadcasted apply-like function. <br /> <br />

</li></ul>

<b>Other functions</b> <br />
'broadcast' provides
[type-casting](typecast.qmd) functions,
which preserve names and dimensions - convenient for arrays. <br />
<br />
'broadcast' also provides
[simple linear algebra functions for statistics](linear_algebra_stats.qmd). <br />
<br />
And 'broadcast' comes with some helper functions: <br />
[bc_dim](bc_dim.qmd), [ndim](ndim.qmd), [lst.ndim](ndim.qmd), [rep_dim](rep_dim.qmd). <br /> <br />



### Overloading

Sometimes broadcasting is needed in a large mathematical expression,
involving multiple variables,
where precedence is of importance. <br />
For example in an expression like <code>x + y / z^y</code>. <br />
For such cases, you may want to overload the base operators. <br />
To that end, the 'broadcast' package provides the [broadcaster](broadcaster.qmd) class attribute,
which comes with its own method dispatch for the base operators. <br /> <br />
